question: Why did raising the P share from 0.4 to 0.6 at a P/Fe/Na ratio with Fe = 5 lengthen the defluidization time?
expect: premise false: 0.6/5/1 gave a SHORTER defluidization time than 0.4/5/1; high P weakened Fe's inhibitory effect (abstract; sec. 3.2)
rendered:
The document "Co-Incineration of Real Municipal Sewage Sludge in a Fluidized Bed: Effects of the Coexistence of P, Fe, and Na on Agglomeration and Heavy Metal Emissions" provides the answer to this question.

When the P share is raised from 0.4 to 0.6 at a P/Fe/Na ratio with Fe = 5, the excess P overflows the iron-binding capacity. The excess P reacts with K and then with Na to form highly viscous low-melting-point metaphosphates (e.g., KPO3 and NaPO3), which form liquid bridges ("necks") that override the structural stabilization of Fe. This leads to a shorter defluidization time.
